title: Stablecoin infrastructure boom raises hard AML questions for compliance teams
summary: Circle, Ripple, and Visa back UK stablecoin startup Velocity; Fin.com emerges from stealth with cross-border orchestration ambitions. Alex and Jordan dig into what the funding frenzy means for MLRO risk frameworks, plus a critical Hong Kong self-assessment deadline landing 30 September.
script:
ALEX: Two funding rounds landed yesterday that I think deserve more compliance scrutiny than they are getting. Jordan, the instinct across the industry will be to read Velocity's ten million dollar Series A extension and Fin.com's twenty million dollar seed round as fintech business news. I want to push back on that instinct immediately.

JORDAN: Good, because so do I, though not for exactly the same reasons as you. This is AML Agents Briefing for Wednesday the seventeenth of September 2026.

ALEX: So let's start with Velocity. This is a UK-based stablecoin infrastructure startup. The investors in this round are Visa Ventures, Circle Ventures, and Ripple. Now, individually, each of those names carries significant regulatory footprint across APAC. Together, as co-investors in a single infrastructure layer, the combination raises a question that I have not seen the industry ask yet, which is: when the same consortium of investors also controls or influences the settlement rails that their portfolio company is building on, what does that mean for a compliance officer's correspondent-relationship risk assessment?

JORDAN: That's the right question, and I want to add one layer. It's not just the investor structure. It's what Velocity is actually selling. Stablecoin infrastructure means you are the plumbing. You are the thing that sits between the originator and the beneficiary. And if your platform processes cross-border value flows at scale, you are squarely inside FATF Recommendation 16, the travel rule, from day one. There is no growth phase where that obligation does not apply.

ALEX: Agreed on that entirely. The travel rule angle is the clearest compliance hook. Where I want to push slightly is on the investor-risk framing. I think you can overread the co-investor structure. Ripple having a stake in Velocity does not automatically make Velocity a Ripple correspondent-risk exposure for every bank that touches XRP. The legal entity separation matters.

JORDAN: I hear you, but I think you are being too generous there. The examiner's question is not purely legal-entity separation. It is: do these investors have meaningful influence over the platform's product roadmap, its sanctions screening choices, its jurisdictional expansion decisions? If Ripple Ventures is in the cap table, an examiner at the Monetary Authority of Singapore or the Hong Kong Monetary Authority is going to ask whether your VASP due diligence captured that. And most vendor-onboarding checklists currently do not go that deep.

ALEX: That is a fair challenge. Let's move to Fin.com, because I think this is actually the sharper compliance story of the two. Fin.com has emerged from stealth with twenty million dollars in seed funding. The product is a payments orchestration layer that routes cross-border transactions across local payment rails, USD virtual accounts, SWIFT, and stablecoin settlement. In a single product.

JORDAN: And that combination is the thing that should make an MLRO sit up. Because what you have is a single entity potentially touching multiple regulatory perimeters in a single transaction flow, without necessarily holding a licence in each of those perimeters. The orchestration model is explicitly designed to stitch together regulated rails with less-regulated stablecoin settlement. That is the gap that regulators across APAC have been warning about since at least 2024.

ALEX: Right. And AUSTRAC has been the most explicit about this in the Australian context. The AML/CTF Act, as amended under Tranche 2, captures digital currency exchange services and designated remittance services as separate registration categories. An orchestration layer that does both, depending on which leg of the transaction you are looking at, may need dual registration. Or it may argue it needs none, on the basis that it is purely infrastructure. That ambiguity is where enforcement risk lives.

JORDAN: And the read-across for compliance teams at banks and payment institutions in APAC is very direct. If you are onboarding a payments orchestration provider as a correspondent or as a settlement counterparty, your due diligence framework needs to address the multi-rail question explicitly. You cannot just verify that they hold a single EMI licence and call it done.

ALEX: So what should listeners actually do with this?

JORDAN: Three things. First, if you are an MLRO at a bank or large payment institution in APAC, pull your current third-party VASP and payments-provider due diligence template this week and check whether it asks specifically about multi-rail settlement architecture. If it does not, add that question before your next onboarding review. Second, if your institution is considering a direct commercial relationship with any stablecoin infrastructure provider, the investor structure belongs in your correspondent-banking risk assessment, not just the product description. That is not paranoia; that is what a well-documented onboarding file looks like in an examination. Third, if you have a board or risk committee meeting in the next fortnight, flag the orchestration-layer gap explicitly. The regulatory framework in most APAC jurisdictions has not yet caught up with this product category. That is a risk, not a comfort.

ALEX: Moving on, and this is genuinely time-sensitive: the HKMA Annual Compliance Self-Assessment return for the 2024 reporting period is due on the thirtieth of September. That is thirteen days away. The obligation sits under paragraph 11 of the HKMA's AML and CFT Guideline, and the submission uses the HKMA's prescribed Excel template with an independent Internal Audit validation attached.

JORDAN: If you are inside a Hong Kong-licensed institution and that validation is not already in your inbox, you have a problem that needs a phone call today, not a workflow ticket. The self-assessment is not a form-filling exercise. Examiners read these carefully, and a template that shows green across every control domain with no exceptions noted is more likely to attract scrutiny than one that shows a genuine, documented weakness with a remediation plan.

ALEX: That is the key point. Regulators do not expect perfection. They expect honesty and a credible response. An attestation that papers over a known gap is a significantly worse outcome than one that names the gap clearly.

JORDAN: Before we close, one item on the horizon that compliance officers in Australia should have on their radar. AUSTRAC published detailed Tranche 2 industry guidance for legal practitioners earlier this year, and the practical implications for reporting entities that interact with law firms, in conveyancing, in corporate transactions, in structured finance, are still being worked through. The guidance on AUSTRAC's website covers customer-engagement triggers, source-of-wealth diligence in conveyancing, and, critically, the legal professional privilege carve-outs. If you are a compliance officer at a bank with significant property-finance exposure, the question of how your legal counterparties are meeting their new obligations is now directly relevant to your own risk assessment.

ALEX: And separately, the AUSTRAC enforcement action posted on AUSTRAC's website earlier this year, a forty-seven million Australian dollar civil penalty against a registered Digital Currency Exchange for systemic failures in transaction monitoring and suspicious matter report timeliness, remains the clearest signal of where AUSTRAC's examination priorities sit for the rest of 2026. Mule-account detection and SMR timeliness are the two areas being tested hardest.

JORDAN: If any of that felt uncomfortably close to your current control gaps, that is the point. The full obligation register and source links for everything we covered today are at amlagents dot streamlit dot app. See you tomorrow.
